Immigration Act, 1976
However, the Government rejected that motion. Therefore, if we are to do anything to flag this problem, the alternative is to vote to delete the clause as a whole. That, of course, is not really the best alternative theoretically or ideally. What would have been best would have been for the Government to have allowed time for the consideration of this legislation.
The Government probably thinks it was very generous in allowing us a week but, in fact, every witness who came before us referred to the difficulty involved in getting a copy of the Bill, studying the Bill and preparing a considered presentation on it. Nevertheless, most of them did speak against this clause.
It would have been better to give the Bill more study. If the Government had slowed down a bit, perhaps it would have been able to think more cooly and calmly about the entire Bill.
The Government did create quite a furor in July with onesided statements about the people who arrived in the ship Amelie. People who came through other means and manners were mixed up in that furor as well, but that furor has considerably cooled off.
If it were possible to continue consideration of the Bill, or if the Government had waited even a few days to allow further consideration of the Bill before taking up positions pro and con in the usual adversarial way of Parliament, I think a better job would have been done on the Bill. The Government chose for its own political purposes to rush the Bill through in the style of an emergency as though it were not 174 unarmed people who arrived on our shores but 174,000 armed troops invading us.
Experts have told us that this clause is a deprivation of the due process of law. It is a deprivation of the normal rights of a detained person to defend his interests, even while the Government pursues its suspicions or accusations.
It has been suggested that it does not do much harm to reduce or even take away the rights of these people because they are strangers. They are not Canadian citizens, nor are they Canadian residents. They are foreigners. They just came here and therefore we have very few obligations to them as far as human rights go.
That is not the position taken by the Supreme Court when dealing with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and it is not the position most Canadians have in fact taken toward strangers. In fact, the first Canadians who met the Amelie offered these people food and drink, throughout the world the traditional way to greet a stranger who may be in difficulty.
Treating strangers with an unusual amount of detention and a refusal of habeas corpus or the related rights of review may seem harmless because it is done to these people who have just arrived and whom the Government expects to get rid of. Of course, the Government is treating them as though guilty until they can prove themselves innocent.
I wish to point out that it is a matter of experience, not over
years but over generations and centuries, that what we do to
other people very often comes back to haunt us. If we deny the human rights and if we deny the humanity of strangers, we have undermined or jeopardized our claim to humanity, that is to say, we have called in question our belief in humanity and in the rights of humanity.
That is why it is risky to pass this law which takes away some, not all, of what our court has considered the basic human right of humanity, not of Canadians only, but of humanity. The court did not extend the application of its decision beyond Canada's borders, quite rightly, but it said that a human within our borders does have certain basic rights simply because of being human and being within our borders.
This law encroaches on that principle. It does not wipe it out entirely but it undermines it. I think it would be a mistake for Parliament to proceed with this law. I think it was a mistake to proceed so hastily with Bill C-84. This is one of the parts that should be withdrawn and given further consideration.
The Justice Department, which may have said it is just fine also said that while the law was just fine, it denied an oral hearing to refugee claimants. The Supreme Court said that that was not just fine. Therefore, the Government is not wise to proceed on the advice of the Justice Department against the advice of many reputable private citizens.
This Government, especially, makes a point of favouring the initiative of private citizens over Government. I wish it would remember that principle it preaches and consider the well credentialed and well respected private citizens who have warned the Government against either the whole of Clause 12 or certain parts of it. Therefore, I support the motion to have this Clause deleted from the Bill.

Mr. Speaker, this is another motion made necessary by a repugnant approach in another portion of this Bill. 1 welcome the presence of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) this afternoon in the House. He has finally found the courage to come here and defend his Bill. We have two Ministers of Immigration but neither has had the guts to defend the Bill during the two days that we have been debating it. They have been hiding behind the Parliamentary Secretary who is carrying the Bill in this House because the Ministers have not had the courage to speak up and explain some of the offensive, nasty, vile and mean clauses it contains. Clause 20 is one of them.
I looked forward to the intervention of the Minister of State for Immigration, hearing his voice in defence of this junk, Mr. Speaker. It is high time the Ministers came out from behind the curtains to defend their own bills instead of hiding behind the Parliamentary Secretary who is carrying the can for them.
We are here on Clause 20. The Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has suggested that it be deleted, as has the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap). They are quite right. In the committee hearings we heard interventions by the civil
September 1, 1987

liberties people, the coalition and other organizations. They told us that clauses like this contain flagrant abuses of the Charter and that they will lead to action in the courts. Before you know it, the very intent of the Government in introducing legislation for the purpose that this Government has found absolutely necessary and urgent will be defeated, because there will be individuals and groups who will find measures such as the one contained in Clause 20 offensive from a constitutional and from the Charter point of view.
The Civil Liberties Association told us in committee that detention, search and seizure provisions probably also violate the Charter of Rights. What is the answer of the Minister to that observation on the part of the Civil Liberties Association?
We spent the morning talking about another measure in this Bill which does not make a distinction, so that people who help refugees for non-profit reasons are going to be brought before the law as criminals. We also argued that that clause ought to be deleted. Clause 20 is another offensive clause.
I think the Minister has an obligation, as a Minister of the Crown, to make sure he is not asking the House of Commons and the other place to pass a piece of legislation that is likely to be tied up in the courts, making this whole exercise futile perhaps for months and months or even for years. The Government has been warned, not just by the Opposition, but by credible well established individuals and organizations, that it is producing poor legislation, to put it mildly. It is seeding the elements for action in the higher courts.
Let us hear from the Minister of State for Immigration who has finally emerged out of nowhere after two days of debate. Let us hear from him as to how he will defend Clause 20 and the preceding clauses which we have brought to the attention of the Government in no uncertain terms.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) for following a certain pattern of logic in his argument. The Member for Spadina asks that the person in question be released. That motion being defeated, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) asked that the entire section be taken out. If we consider it a security risk to relieve the person in question with which that section deals, how much greater is it a security risk to do away with the section altogether? There really is not much logic based upon this particular motion before us.
While I understand exactly from where the Hon. Member for Spadina is coming, it really does not help to accuse the Government by saying that it does not do much harm to take away the rights of strangers and foreigners. I would hope that the Member for Spadina would not make light accusations like that.
Immigration Act, 1976
This section is here mainly to protect the rights of strangers and foreigners. If I could point out to the Member that the present Immigration Act, to which the Hon. Member for York West likes to refer and to which he would like to return, allows an immigration officer, without issue of a warrant, to detain people. The present provisions require the Minister to have a certificate based upon hard evidence presented in order to do that.
It seems to me that what we are doing in this section is preserving the not only Canadian security and the rights of Canadian individuals, but is, in effect and in fact, protecting the civil rights of the person being detained. A person cannot be detained willy-nilly at the whim of an immigration officer. There has to be conclusive evidence to believe that he is a risk. 1 hope the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) will be a little bit more careful about heavy accusations made lightly.
Since this motion would effectively emasculate the Canadian immigration security system we cannot support it.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary suggests that if this clause is removed we will have no system for monitoring those who wish to come to this country. He also says the current Act has these kinds of provisions. What he and the Minister do not want to face up to is the fact that it is not just opposition Members of Parliament who are critical of this Bill and this clause. It is just about everyone who has ever been interested in the question of immigration and refugees and who wants Canada to continue to take a humane and generous approach to both subjects.
This Bill was drafted and introduced by the Government in a hurry because it perceived that as a result of this last movement into Canada by ship of a fairly substantial number of Sikhs the public had turned against a humane and generous policy. In fact, that view was very temporarily held. Every single organization which can claim to represent large numbers of people and which can honestly and justifiably say it wants Canada to be generous has expressed its opposition to this Bill and this clause. I want to bring to the attention of the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary the information contained in an article which appeared in today's Globe and Mail. When we oppose this Bill we speak for a large number of people. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Johnny Carson.

Sits over there.
I was going to say that this is probably the most important motion, i am pleased that the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) is in the House. Like my colleague, the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), I welcome him and urge him, rather than his Parliamentary Secretary, to respond to some of these concerns at report stage.
Motion No. 23 contains a sunset clause which would give this legislation a lifespan of six months, after which time this Parliament would be able to review the workability of the policy, strike out clauses which are offensive and clearly unworkable, and retain those clauses which are reflective of
September 1, 1987

our international obligations-which are probably few and far between-and of our Charter of Rights.
The sunset clause motion is moved as a result of a number of groups, including the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Civil Liberties Association and Rabbi Plaut, advocating it to the committee. It is fitting that we examine the reasons for this clause. There are three reasons for which I suggest that the Government should support this sunset clause.
The first is that most of the amendments presented by the Opposition and witnesses at committee have gone unheard. Amendments were suggested to allow priests, nuns, and other innocent Canadians who aid legitimate refugees coming in to this country to be exempt from fines and imprisonment. Amendments were suggested to allow boats loaded with refugees to be escorted into port, to allow for due processing of the passengers, the return of any passengers who have protection in other countries, the impounding of the boat, and the charging of the captain, thereby deterring other smugglers who would follow the same course.
The Bill still contains unnecessary detainment and deportation clauses. The existing legislation protects our country from undesirables and contains checks and balances to ensure that the rights of individual human beings are not infringed upon. The witnesses who suggested those amendments said that if their amendments were not accepted for the long term, at the very least at the eleventh hour let Parliament give this Bill a lifespan of only six months.
The second aspect is to try to avoid the Charter challenges which every legal expert and witness who came before the committee predicted would be made at the first opportunity by lawyers across the land.
Parliament was called back under the guise of an emergency. The Government has whipped up public frenzy to try to justify its own actions. What will happen 12, 16 or 18 months hence? What will the Government and the Minister of State for Immigration tell Canadians when this piece of legislation is gobbled up by the courts? What will the Minister say when the policy is paralyzed?
Canadians trusted the Government to pass a proper and fitting piece of legislation which would deal with the abuses while protecting rights and civil liberties and keeping the legislation out of the courts. How is the Government going to promote a more progressive immigration policy when every Canadian has lost confidence because this policy has been paralyzed and rendered null and void by the courts?
Apart from not listening to the amendments, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and his officials have refused to make public their legal opinion on this Bill. Until we exerted pressure in the House of Commons during Question Period, Justice officials refused to come before the legislative committee studying Bill C-84.
Immigration Act, 1976
The implication of that is clear. It is obvious that the Department of Justice does not want to defend the indefensible. It knows that this Bill, drafted as poorly as it was, will not meet the test of our Charter and of our Constitution. I believe that the Government knows that, but it is willing to continue nonetheless. It will enjoy short-term gain in return for long-term political pain.
Charter challenges should be avoided. As a legislature we should take our responsibility of drafting proper legislation seriously. If we do not, the Government will pay a much higher price than it would pay now by accepting a number of sensible amendments.
The third and final reason for this sunset clause is in response to the Government's suggestion that it has introduced emergency legislation. My definition of an emergency is "short term", "temporary". An emergency does not last forever. Therefore, it is not necessary for emergency legislation to become permanent. Emergency legislation implies that the new revamped system which we hope to provide through Bill C-55 in an amended form will give us a system of refugee determination that will make Bill C-84 useless and redundant.
The best deterrent to any individual is a processing system of less than six months. No one will spend $15,000 and go to much trouble and pain to come to our shores if they know they will be able to stay for a maximum of only six months. The system presently takes years and, therefore, they take their chances. The ultimate deterrent is a proper, fair and expeditious determination system. If we put that into place, Bill C-84 will not be needed.
It is for those three reasons, Mr. Speaker, that we are suggesting at this eleventh hour at report stage that if the Government really wants to proceed without listening to the amendments suggested by Canadians it should put the legislation into force for only six months and allow Parliament and Canadians to determine the future course of the legislation.
I will conclude with a quote from Gunther Plaut. Some Members did not hear his testimony and I urge them to read it because he offered a very forceful and moving presentation. He said:
Treat the stranger fairly; you should extend your love and friendship to him. Remember that you too were strangers once.
1 think that Draconian and emergency legislation gives the wrong signal, not only to the world but it gives the wrong word to our own people in Canada. 1 ask you to look carefully at some of the amendments suggested. Do not follow the worst instincts of people, follow the best instincts.
1 think the Bill was drawn in undue haste. This is why 1 think we need just a little more leisure to write legislation that makes sense.
I believe that the sunset clause for six months is more than a valiant compromise because there are principles here that are tough to swallow. If the legislation is only on the books for six months, at least it allows our country and this Parliament to

September 1, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
escape with some degree of integrity. If it is permanent, longterm legislation, no dignity can possibly be salvaged from this legislation.
I sincerely request the Minister of State to reflect on this proposition. Perhaps, after he has heard the Member from the New Democratic Party and my colleague, the Member or Davenport, he will give the House a proper answer and send a signal to those Canadians who requested this clause that their concerns are being adhered to and their input counts for something.

Mr. Speaker, coincidentally, I have a motion on the same subject although its content is different. I was quite happy to let the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) proceed first because he has an urgent engagement.
I will support his motion even though I have a different motion in case this one should fail. I support the motion and recommend that our Party should support it, somewhat in the same sporting vein as was traditional with soldiers in World War I who were signed up for four years or the duration, whichever was shorter. I am willing to try six months or the duration of this Government. According to the newspapers, I think this may come to a test soon, and I am not sure which would be the quickest way to get rid of this Bill. In the meantime, I will support the motion of the Hon. Member for York West.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the principle of a sunset clause has been described by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi).
I wish to make only two points in support of my motion which is, in effect, a two-year sunset clause. First, I believe the general principle of a two-year sunset clause is good. I give credit to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) for having first introduced an amendment in committee that would have brought the sunset at five years and for amending her own amendment to bring it down to four years. She had a good idea and was moving in the right direction. I would simply like to move it a bit farther.
I agree with the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary that six months would hardly give enough time for the public to realize what a very bad law this is. I believe two years would really convince the public that the Government, whether it was then in operation or not, had erred very badly. As an illustration of that, let me quote from a source that I hope the Hon. Member will not regard as biased in a hostile way. It is the Calgary Herald of August 26, which contains an editorial with the heading "Amending a Hasty Law".
It states that Bill C-84 is a bad law "because it will not in some respects deter abuse and because it is so sweepingly vague that it almost certainly violates the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, international treaties Canada has signed, and the rights of refugee support groups within Canada".
It goes on to state that the law "needs to spell out who is deemed to be involved in smuggling illegal immigrants".
One of the remarkable features of this Bill is that the Minister advertised for weeks ahead that it would stop smugglers. While the Minister talks about stopping smugglers in the first clause of the Bill, smugglers and smuggling are not mentioned in the Bill.
September 1, 1987

A smuggler is a person who brings somebody in, usually by stealth, but at any rate in violation of the laws. That is not spelled out in the Bill.
The editorial goes on to say that it should spell out who is deemed to be involved in smuggling illegal aliens for profit and make clear that it will in no way affect the activities of refugee jppporters who aid those who legitimately flee persecution for safe haven in Canada.
Of course, those are amendments that the Government has refused to make, as I am sure the Calgary Herald takes note.
The editorial goes on to state that Bill C-84 traps the people who aid legitimate refugees while failing to spell out the crimes and punishments aimed at unscrupulous so-called immigration consultants who advise people in foreign lands to use the refugee stream as a means of coming to Canada. They may be pleased with Section 95.4 which arose out of our discussions and which was moved and therefore supported by the Government. At least it remembered for a week.
The editorial went on to state: "The detention provisions which allow officials to hold claimants for 28 days and longer without hearings deny the basic concept of habeas corpus".
I commend the editorial to the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary. The Calgary Herald is not one of the pressure groups or one of those who perhaps has a stake in this. I do not know whether the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary considers the Calgary Herald guilty of romanticism and wanting to race down to the American border for the fun of bringing across a refugee. I am not familiar with the Calgary Herald, but I hope the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary would give some consideration to their view.
I hope he would support my motion for a two-year sunset clause because I suggest it gives a fair chance to find out whether this law is really attacking the people whom the Government originally said it wanted to attack or whether it is attacking those whom the Government said it does not want to attack while missing the real smugglers.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the reasoning and the motivation of the Hon. Member or Spadina (Mr. Heap) in trying to contain and manage the duration of this piece of legislation. Therefore, I understand his desire to put forward a motion for a sunset clause. The more 1 thought about it as I was listening to him, the more convinced 1 became that the sun will set on this Government at the next election and take care of the nefarious legislation and policies it has introduced during this Parliament, not just in terms of social policy but in terms of economic policies. There will be the day when the sun will set and take care of the ideology that is emanating from those benches opposite.
I am still waiting to hear from the Minister for Employment. The Government has two Ministers for that portfolio and the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) sits
Immigration Act, 1976
there reading his correspondence and perhaps signing Christmas cards, but has not entered into this debate in defence of his own piece of legislation. It is the second day of debate on this measure and we have not heard one peep out of the Minister of State for Immigration. He is hiding behind mother Friesen's skirts rather than standing up in his place and telling us why he is introducing some of these repugnant clauses in this piece of legislation. This legislation has prompted the Hon. Member for Spadina to rise in his place and ask for a sunset clause, and my colleague the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) is asking for a similar measure. The only difference is that one period of time is longer than the other.
This is the extent of the repugnance this Bill has awakened in the Opposition. As the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) mentioned earlier, this repugnance is not only felt by the Opposition.
It is reported in the Ottawa Citizen and in the Globe and Mail that a group of outstanding citizens met in the capital yesterday. They are not members of dangerous political movements, nor are they crypto Communists or radicals on the left, who came out and spoke against this Bill. They are a group of citizens which included the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, and the like. Anglican Archbishop Edward Scott, the President of the Canadian Council of Churches, is quoted as accusing the Government at the press conference of orchestrating an emergency. He suggested that there is clear evidence that the Government knew for some time that the boat was on its way. He is asking that this Bill be scrapped.
This is not the Opposition speaking. It is a group of citizens from across the nation speaking against this measure which is so outrageous in the context of some of the clauses we have been debating for two days. Not one but two Ministers of Immigration have been silent on this legislation, asking the Parliamentary Secretary to deliver the goods for them. The Government is hiding behind him. What kind of management is this? What a shame. What a lack of guts it takes to handle a piece of legislation in this manner.
In my 19 years in this House of Commons I have not seen a piece of legislation managed in this way. I cannot recall one instance when the Minister did not come into the House on a contested piece of legislation to defend it. I have never seen that before. In most instances we would only have one Minister, but here we have two Ministers and not one of the two has spoken at report stage despite the number of amendments which were brought forward.
What can we say? The Hon. Member for Spadina has done a very thorough job. The Hon. Member for York West has worked very hard with his amendments. There are about 23 amendments. We have now reached the end of report stage and I invite the Minister of State for Immigration to rise in his

place and say something about these amendments, if he has the guts to speak.

Second, I want to say that I agree with the principle of the Hon. Member's motion. As he pointed out, the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Collins) has already taken care of that principle in the legislation by introducing at committee stage a review clause which at first called for a five-year review and, as the Hon. Member pointed out, it was reduced in committee to four years. I think that is a reasonable length of time.
As I say, I can agree totally with the Hon. Member's principle, and that is a review of the legislation, because world circumstances change and domestic circumstances change. It is wholesome to review the provisions of the Bill in that context. However, I do think it is unrealistic to think of reviewing the legislation in two years. There are far too many undulations of circumstances. There is just not enough time to see the effects of the legislation through the administration of the Bill.
Therefore, I think it is impractical to think of a review process after two years of implementation. I would hold to the four year provision we passed in committee.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to add my voice to those concerned about this legislation which will remove Canagrex from the Canadian landscape.
There are a number of points I want to make. First and foremost, it comes at a rather opportune time. By any definition, a crisis in agriculture is pending or has arrived. The delegations which appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture over the last number of weeks made it perfectly clear that agriculture is at a very important point. There are some basic decisions that the Government and the Parliament of Canada must make. Are we going to take significant initiatives, unfortunately in some cases remedial action, to ensure that the family farm or family ranch remains a viable institution on the agricultural landscape of Canada? Or are we prepared to turn our back on rural Canada and turn it over to agri-business or corporate agriculture? Around the world some countries have made that decision. Some decided that the family farm as a production unit is worth preserving. As a result, they put in place a variety of programs to make that possible.
It is an incredibly competitive world and, in many respects, the competition is unfair. We are asking our farmers and ranchers to compete in a very unfair market-place. Heavy subsidies are given to the European farm community which make it virtually impossible for our producers to compete on international markets. Then we have the spectre of free trade talks and the possibility, because none of us really know what is going on, of initiatives which would result in the American agricultural community moving in to Canada and simply taking over. I refer specifically to the case made by poultry producers, egg producers, dairy producers, and a number of other sectors of the agricultural community who are very serious about the potential influence of a free trade agreement on their area.
I come from central British Columbia where agriculture
plays an important role. The rural fabric of that area is
dependent upon a healthy and viable agricultural community.
We have the soft fruit industry, the hard fruit industry, the vineyards of the Okanagan Valley, and then the more exotic crops such as ginseng which are aimed at far eastern markets. We have traditional cattle ranching and vegetable producers who are just beginning, under incredibly competitive conditions, to make successful inroads into new markets. This is often done with the assistance of the provincial Government, the federal Government, and in some cases even local Governments.
Today we are discussing the abandonment of Canagrex. It is important that we remind ourselves what Canagrex was all about. It was an initiative taken by the federal Government to market Canadian agricultural products in a more effective and efficient way in new areas. Our food producers are among the most efficient in the world. They can compete in the international market-place. However, they have often required some assistance. The farmer raising a certain type of oil-seed, or a farmer raising rabbits or raspberries, whatever the crop may be, does not have the time or the capacity to go to Japan to develop a market.
Some other Hon. Members of this place and I had the good fortune to visit Japan some time back. We looked at the potential for Canadian food producers in that market. We learned that they are very pleased with the quality of foodstuffs from Canada. Not surprisingly, we found a considerable potential. As a matter of fact, wherever we went, food fairs were being conducted by our embassy introducing the Japanese to Canadian foods and recipes. The response was fantastic. That is why we feel that wherever Canadians have made the effort to develop and expand markets overseas for our food producers, it has been successful. Yet it is costly and time-consuming.
That was the point of Canagrex. It had a very modest budget to go out and sell our products overseas. A lot of people have asked why our farmers cannot do that. Obviously they do not have time or necessarily the expertise. Often their organizations are limited by their funding. We said, "Let us put aside a Crown corporation to do that for our food producers. They deserve nothing less. Let us put in place a mechanism whereby Canagrex is evaluated on a regular basis. Get farmers on the board of directors. Hold it accountable for its actions." It was a very progressive piece of work. Then, just as it was beginning its work and opening up new markets, providing hundreds and potentially tens of thousands of jobs, both directly and in supporting industries, what did the Government do? It pulled the rug out and decided to abandon it. It did so because, when it was set up, the Progressive Conservatives were in opposition.
I recall them going on at some length about how this was not necessary, our farmers did not require that support. I do not think they said that farmers did not deserve the support, but they did say that they did not require it.
The success of Canagrex was something to behold. If anyone
sat down and objectively evaluated what that small Crown
corporation did in a very short period of time, it was nothing
September 1, 1987

short of remarkable. Dedicated people wanted to see our agricultural sector expand.
It is with some reluctance that I discuss this today. It is with some sadness and sorrow that I have to comment on the deathbed of Canagrex. We have one more spike to drive into its coffin, and I guess that is in a sense what we are doing. However, I want to remind my friends on the government side that now is the time we need to rally behind the family farm. Now is the time to rally behind the food producers of Canada. Therefore, I plead at this last moment for my friends in the Conservative caucus to reconsider the abandonment of this initiative to assist Canadian food producers.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING PEACE IN CENTRAL AMERICA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of sponsoring a major initiative to enhance the opportunities for peace in Central America through steps including, but not necessarily limited to:
1.	appointing a personal envoy of the Prime Minister to reinforce diplomatic efforts regionally and internationally;
2.	establishing an embassy in Nicaragua;
3.	establishing a "Peace Fund", with contributions from like-minded Western nations, to cover costs associated with implementation of the Contadora treaty; and
4.	introducing at the UN a General Assembly Resolution calling on the Secretary-General to dispatch a civilian monitoring commission to the region.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak today on a motion that I introduced on June 19 of this year which calls on the Canadian Government to take specific and concrete steps to assist in the peace process in Central America. These steps, combined with some other suggestions which I am about to make, would amount to a major Canadian diplomatic initiative.
I hope that the Government will take seriously the possibility of a diplomatic initiative. Such a move would reinforce the initiatives that thousands of Canadians have been taking for many years and continue to undertake today.
In many of the Central American countries there are Canadians working for a just and lasting peace in practical and concrete ways. There are many Canadians in Canada working for charitable and solidarity projects in support of the
Peace in Central America
people of Central America. I hope the Government will take seriously the initiative of so many concerned Canadians by responding with an initiative of its own.
1 do not want to suggest for an instant that the Government has done nothing to promote a genuine Canadian desire for peace or Canadian action for peace. I want to acknowledge, for example, that the Government has offered technical assistance to the countries of Central America for peacekeeping and verification. I want to commend the Government for voting against Mr. Reagan in the United Nations on the motion calling on the U.S. to obey the international law and honour the International Court injunction against the mining of the harbours of Nicaragua. I want to recognize that the Government has provided both bilateral aid and assistance to nongovernmental organizations to the Central American nations.
However, these actions do not amount to the kind of diplomatic initiative that Canada could and should take. I would like my suggestions to be taken as friendly suggestions and my criticism as constructive.
The weeks since I introduced this motion have been exciting ones. They were full of hope for the peoples of Central America and their sympathizers and supporters here in Canada. A peace plan has been adopted by the Central American Governments. Momentum for peace is growing. There are many obstacles to a just and lasting peace. Anything that Canada can do to help increase the momentum for peace must be done.
That increased momentum began, as you know, with the August 7 signing of an accord between the Presidents of the five Central American nations. This accord was reached despite the extensive last-minute efforts by Mr. Reagan to scuttle the talks. Some commentators have suggested, as a matter of fact, that his untimely intervention may have solidified the will of the Central American leaders to accomplish their own peace plan. This week we have seen some signs that Honduras may be showing cold feet, and Mr. Reagan has made it clear that he wishes to keep fighting in Nicaragua. It is clear that there are obstacles to peace for Central America.
The Foreign Ministers have made progress in their meetings in San Salvador. They are organizing working groups necessary to implement the various provisions of the agreement; the cease-fires, the amnesties, the end to guerrilla bases in one country for attack on another, the restoration of civil rights, a free press, and free elections throughout the region. This accomplishment may help overcome some of the obstacles to peace.
Eight other Latin American nations have been asked to sit on a regional peace commission to supervise the process. The United Nations and the Organization of American States will be part of this commission. In El Salvador the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front has agreed to meet with President Jose Napoleon Duarte on September 15 to discuss a cease fire. In Nicaragua the Sandanista Government has appointed the Cardinal of the Catholic church, Miguel

September 1, 1987
Peace in Central America
Obando y Bravo, to serve on a commission of national reconciliation. Cardinal Obando is and has been a fervent critic of the Sandinista Government.
Also on that commission will be Mauricio Diaz Davila, leader of the popular Social Christian Party. Mr. Diaz will represent the largest block of opposition Parties in the legislature. The third member will be Dr. Gustavo Parajon, a physician and Baptist missionary who heads the Protestant Committee for Aid and Development. The Government will be represented by the vice President of Nicaragua, Sergio Ramirez. This commission may be able to overcome some of the obstacles to peace.
Unhappily, it is clear that Mr. Reagan is still looking for ways to scuttle the peace accord. He has dispatched a swarm of diplomats to the region. He has spoken on the Contra radio station. He has threatened to continue military aid to the terrorists even after the cease fire comes into force. Perhaps most important, he is leaning on governments in the region, particularly those of Honduras and El Salvador, to back out of the accord. This is unforgivable interference on the part of the Reagan administration and makes a mockery of Mr. Reagan's supposed interest in promoting peace in Central America.
Fortunately, in the aftermath of the Contragate hearings, the Central American accord gives the Democratic majority in the U.S. House of Representatives good grounds on which to limit or reject additional funding for the Contra terrorists when the current funding runs out in September.
For some time in the wake of Colonel North's testimony it looked as though American public opinion might be shifting towards supporting the Contras. However, I am pleased to report that according to the latest New York Times-CBS news poll only 33 per cent of Americans support such aid while half of Americans oppose it. There truly are obstacles to a fair and just peace in Central America, but there are also hopeful signs and a growing momentum for peace.
As a nation with an international reputation for peacekeeping and peacemaking Canada can help build on this momentum. We owe it to our Central American neighbours to do all we can to assist. They have suffered war and violence for too many years.
What can Canada do? We can help to mobilize international opinion. We can lend our moral suport to the people of Central America. We can lend practical support. We can make a difference. Canadians can help bring an end to those bloody wars. We can help to build a just and lasting peace.
In my motion submitted to the House on June 19 I first suggested that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should send a personal envoy to Central America to reinforce our diplomatic efforts. In fact, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) sent not one but two envoys to offer Canada's technical expertise in peacekeeping and verification.
This is a very practical form of aid which Canada has provided. I applaud that move and hope that the Minister will take up more New Democrat suggestions.
My second suggestion was that Canada should take a leading role in establishing a peace fund with contributions from western nations to help with the costs of implementation. Such a move would have both practical and diplomatic significance. Practically, the peace process, and especially the verification process, will cost money. We cannot expect the Reagan administration to make the same financial contribution to peace as it has to war. Diplomatically, such a move would send a clear signal of support to all parties in the region. I ask the Minister to seize this unparalleled opportunity.
My third suggestion was that the Canadian Government should introduce a resolution in the United Nations General Assembly in support of the Central American peace process. Representatives of the United Nations and the Organization of American States will sit on the Regional Verification Commission. These representatives are important in both symbolic and practical terms.
A United Nations General Assembly resolution would present the opportunity to mobilize international opinion. It would send another signal to the participants in this bloody conflict. It would signal international approval of the peace process. It would also signal a Canadian commitment to international law and international organizations as being crucial to peace.
My final suggestion is that Canada establish an embassy in Nicaragua. The Government has argued that our interests are adequately served by our embassy in San Jose, Costa Rica. Without casting aspersions on our embassy staff in Costa Rica, I can assure you that this claim is not well founded.
I was in Nicaragua with a parliamentary delegation in April of this year. Our embassy in Costa Rica organized a dinner so that we could meet the Canadians who are resident in Nicaragua, most of whom are working with non-governmental organizations in Canada or Nicaragua to help the people of Nicaragua. It was a good event and I commend the embassy for organizing it, but I was surprised, as they were, to discover that our embassy had no idea of how many Canadians were in Nicaragua. That is one small example of the lack of knowledge that our Government has about the realities of life in the most controversial country in Central America.
The Government is not even in contact with Canadians who work in Nicaragua and know the country. In case of emergency, moreover, Canadians in Nicaragua are expected to go to the American embassy for assistance in spite of the protests that many of them made against such advice. Given the divergence of U.S. and Canadian policy on that country, this is a very regrettable situation. Our embassy in Costa Rice is expected to cover our interest in Costa Rica, Nicaragua, El
September 1, 1987

Salvador and Panama. In a region as volatile as Central America, it is too much to expect of the staff.
An embassy in Nicaragua would give our Government much more direct and complete information than it can get now. An embassy would enable Canada to engage in continuing and ongoing discussions with the Nicaraguan Government and the Nicaraguan people on matters of mutual concern. The goodwill created by the involvement of hundreds of individual Canadians can provide the base for our officials to have a real influence in Nicaragua.
Finally, an embassy would help promote trade between Nicaragua and Canada, trade that would be to both countries' advantage.
I have suggested moves that would be the beginning of a major diplomatic and practical initiative by Canada to promote and support peace in Central America. It would help to increase momentum for the peace process in Central America. It would be a positive response to the desires of thousands of Canadians who have, through their activities in Canadian solidarity organizations and non-governmental organizations, worked hard, sometimes risking their lives, to help the people of Central America.
This is an opportunity that Canada cannot afford to miss. The people of Central America deserve a just and lasting peace. Canadians can be and deserve to be known as peacemakers.
In addition to the steps I have suggested to the Government in my motion, there are other practical steps the Government should take. For example, we can make use of our bilateral aid program in the name of peace, just as Mr. Reagan does in the name of war. We can make it a condition of our aid that recipient countries adhere to the terms of the peace accord, which calls upon Central American countries to refuse their territory as bases for attacks on other countries.
Members will know that I primarily refer there to El Salvador and Honduras, since both Costa Rica recently, and Nicaragua some years ago, ceased to allow rebel bases on their territories.
Honduras is our major bilateral aid recipient in the region. Honduras has received some $37 million in Canadian aid over the last five years. Honduras is also the country most likely to violate the accord. Members of the Honduran military Government and business classes make money from skimming American aid to the Contras. The American bilateral aid program is clearly dependent on Honduran aid to the Contras. Eleven U.S.-built airstrips and almost continuous U.S. military manoeuvres dominate the economic and political posture of Honduras. Therefore, Honduras must choose. It can choose to conform to a posture set by the Reagan administration, or it can choose to honour its commitment to the peace process. Canada can help to make that choice easier.
We can link our aid to the participation of Honduras in the peace process. Of course, we cannot hope unilaterally to match
Peace in Central America
the amount of aid that the U.S. provides, but we might be able to approach other countries in our hemisphere and in Europe, inviting them to put together an aid package-a sort of consortium for peace.
These are practical steps that would help overcome some of the obstacles to peace. But even if the countries of Central America are allowed to end the fighting without outside interference, efforts must still be made to ensure that peace is peace with justice. For without justice, there can be no lasting peace in Central America or anywhere else. The roots of war lie in injustice. We must learn from history.
Canadians are deeply committed to peace with justice in Central America. I have seen the commitment of Canadians when I visited the region, where I witnessed individual Canadians and Canadian organizations deeply committed to peace with justice. In Guatemala earlier this summer, I witnessed a woman of Guatemalan origin marching with the Organization of Mothers of the Disappeared, demanding an account of their relatives.
In Nicaragua this spring, I visited a young Canadian apiarist working with CARE Canada to help Nicaraguan farmers improve both their honey and crop yields. I visited farming co-ops, where Canadians were helping Nicaraguans improve their farming technique. A similar co-op, after being assisted by an Alberta group, Farmers for Peace, was attacked by Contras earlier this summer. Ten Nicaraguans were killed, four kidnapped, and many houses and buildings burned. The Secretary of State for External Affairs made a very strong protest against that action by the Contras and let the United States Government know of its protest.
Other Canadian projects have been attacked by Contras in Nicaragua as well. Last summer, for instance, a group of Ontario teachers travelled to the mountains to build a school in a remote village. Having made their contribution to the literacy program in Nicaragua, they returned home. Unfortunately, as they waited at the airport in Managua, word came that the Contras had burned the newly built school. Such are the acts of terror committed by the Contras, which the President of the United States continues to finance.
Canadians have put their lives on the line in support of the people of Central America. Earlier this summer, Professor George Sorger and Barbara Paleczny, associated with Amnesty International, visited El Salvador to investigate the numerous reports of human rights violations in that country. On their return, they were picked up and held by Honduran soldiers who threatened them with torture and stole the notes they had made in El Salvador. Fortunately, they were released unharmed.
In El Salvador on July 31, a group of Canadian teachers visiting the village of San Jose Las Flores were seized by government troops, held overnight, and denied medical attention for a sick colleague. I would like to quote from their report:

September 1, 1987
Peace in Central America
We were not prepared for the graphic details supplied by the soldiers, of the
process of torture within the treasury police.
Canadians in this country are doing their part to build a just and lasting peace. As the New Democratic critic for Central American issues, I receive a constant stream of phone calls and correspondence on Central America. Many Canadians are well informed and knowledgeable.
Canadians here in Ottawa have twinned a day care centre, the Glebe Day Care, with a child care centre in Managua. Part of the funds raised by the Glebe Day Care are used to help their counterparts in Managua.
In British Columbia, fishermen are donating their time to build a prototype fishing boat to help modernize the Nicaragua fishing industry.
From one end of this country to the other, thousands of volunteers with tools for peace collect material goods, including blankets for hospitals, notebooks for schools, and money for tin to put roofs on houses, that is shipped from Vancouver to supply material needs in Nicaragua.

In May of this year I attended a conference on peace in Central America here in Ottawa which was organized by Canadians. This conference brought government, academic and other representatives to Ottawa from Honduras, Nicaragua, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Mexico, Peru and other Latin American countries, and from Europe, to discuss the peace process. This conference may well have contributed to preparing the way for the peace accord.
Many of these projects are small by themselves but they have a cumulative impact. They provide practical support for the peoples of Central America. They provide symbolic support for the people to people level. They help to educate Canadians and help to build momentum for peace.
There is a Canadian initiative for peace, an intiative of the Canadian people. I am asking that there also be a distinct Canadian Government initiative for peace in Central America.
I challenge this Government to show the kind of courage and imagination, the kind of dedication and vision that is shown by so many Canadians.
