speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in the House today about the progress made in achieving peace in Central America. In fact, progress is the correct word, if we consider recent events.
As Hon. Members are aware, the Presidents of five Central
American countries recently agreed to a new peace plan for
the region, with the support of the main parties concerned
outside the region, namely the U.S., Cuba and the USSR. This is a very positive development.
However, I do not want to give the impression that the plan is a cure-all for the region's problems. In recent years, negotiations conducted by the countries of the Contadora group-Mexico, Panama, Colombia and Venezuela-have too often raised expectations and been followed by disillusionment and disappointment, which of course in no way diminishes the efforts of the Contadora group which, despite tremendous obstacles, has demonstrated its resolve and determination.
The most serious obstacle would seem to be the existence of serious socio-economic differences. Another obstacle to peace is the guerillas in El Salvador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. Finally, and this may be a decisive factor, we have the power struggle between the two superpowers, which tends to aggravate regional conflicts. Canada sincerely hopes that the goodwill shown by all parties in recent weeks will be reflected in a sincere effort to overcome these obstacles.
Canada has a clear-cut policy with respect to the situation in Central America. In a speech last year before the InterAmerican Press Association, the Prime Minister referred to the Contadora initiative as the best instrument for reconciliation in Central America. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) also said in public statements, in Canada and abroad, that Canada firmly supported the Contadora process. The Secretary of State for External Affairs repeated his position during visits to Argentina, Uruguay and Venezuela in 1986.
In January 1987, in a message addressed to Foreign Affairs Ministers of the Contadora group and the Lima support group, and to the Secretaries General of the United Nations and the Organization for American States on the occasion of their visit to the Central American countries, the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that the efforts of the Contadora group had sustained the hopes of the international community for a lasting solution to the crisis in Central America. In 1986, the Canadian delegation to the UN General Assembly made a statement in support of the Contadora group.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, Canada has provided constructive and practical support for the Contadora group and the general peace process. During his visit to Mexico in 1985, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was able to discuss the situation in Central America and the Contadora group's plan with President de la Madrid and the Minister of Foreign Affairs. He restated Canada's firm support for the Contadora initiative and its desire to play a constructive role in the peace process, when appropriate. The Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that Canada was prepared to share its experience in peacekeeping operations with the parties concerned. Since then, the Canadian Government, at the request of the Contadora group countries, has drafted a series of comments on the provisions of the Draft Convention on Security and Verification.
September 1, 1987

Those comments are based on a number of considerations, including the need to speak in a neutral, objective and unbiased way. We were also aware of the need to ensure the viability of any verification and follow-up commission that may be established under the Contadora Act. Specifically, we thought that the funding for such an operation should be carefully examined by all parties in order that the selected mechanism be as viable as possible, given the circumstances.

We believe that the concept of a regional solution to the current problem should be emphasized. In this regard we believe that the Central American parties themselves ought to be brought into the peacekeeping mechanisms as far as possible. As far as this contributes to the effective operation of a control and verification commission, the commission should enjoy specific and firm guarantees relating to its freedom of movement and access to the region. The commission's role should also permit free and open communication with the media as its members deem appropriate.
Finally, we believe there is a need to designate a sponsoring political authority for the commission and to establish a time limit for the mandate of the commission itself. The Government believes that the principles which were enunciated two years ago for control and verification can be usefully applied to the current peace plan.
On August 7, at the close of their historic summit meeting in Guatemala, the Central American Presidents announced that an agreement had been reached on a new peace plan for Central America. The plan called for a meeting of the foreign Ministers within 15 days to begin implementing an amnesty for insurgents, a cease-fire and dialogue with unarmed opposition groups. This was all to be achieved in 90 days, that is, by November 7. The Contradora countries were to be asked to design and implement a control and verification commission to supervise forest levels in the region.
We were delighted at this breakthrough agreement. Canada's support was made clear on the very day the agreement was signed, and a press release was issued by the Minister for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). The Minister subsequently dispatched two officials to the region during the week of August 17 to demonstrate Canada's support and to offer technical advice on the design of the peacekeeping mechanisms. The visit and the Canadian offer were warmly welcomed by all countries in the region.
There have been further hopeful signs. The agreement, as 1 have said, called for a Foreign Ministers' meeting within 15 days. That meeting took place on August 19 and 20 in San Salvador. The Foreign Ministers then met with their Contadora counterparts, as well as with Foreign Ministers from the Fima support group, and UN and OAS representatives in Caracas on August 22 and 23. They agreed to establish a verification commission.
Peace in Central America
Canada, being outside the Fatin American area, is not a member of the commission. However, we have told all the Governments concerned that we stand ready to offer technical advice to the commission should its members wish us to do so.
I think we can safely conclude therefore that there has been real progress. That is clear from the fact that all five Central American presidents approved the Guatemala plan, demonstrating an unprecedented commitment and the political will to overcome the obstacles. We should be realistic, however, as to the limits of this progress. The guerilla wars continue, as does the superpower competition. The conditions of poverty persist and are exacerbated by massive flows of refugees who have been displaced by the conflicts. Respect for human rights, civil liberties and democratic institutions is still lacking in parts of the region.
This recent progress constitutes a positive but tentative step down a very long road. In this context, international support is vital to maintaining the momentum of the peace process. The Canadian Government will continue to provide encouragement, support and appropriate technical advice deemed useful by the Central American and Contadora countries.
Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, the intent behind this resolution to promote peace in Central America is good but, as has been recognized by its mover and by the speaker for the Government, it is out of date to a certain extent. It is out of date because the five principal countries in Central America concluded a peace agreement in Guatemala City on August 7, 1987, in which they provided for a cease-fire of civil wars within the countries of the region. In particular, that means civil wars in Nicaragua, Salvador and Guatemala. They also provided for a return to democratic government in these countries, as well as an amnesty for opponents of the Government. This means amnesty for the Contras in Nicaragua, as well as amnesty for members of the FMFN in El Salvador and in Guatemala. They provided for a halt to aid to insurgents from outside the country, which would mean stopping American aid to the Contras toward Nicaragua, a halt to any aid from Cuba or the Soviet Union to Nicaragua and, perhaps, to the insurgents in Salvador. Also, the countries that are signatories to the agreement renounced the use of their territory as a basis for struggle against neighbouring countries.
This is a very hopeful agreement. The signatories to the agreement stated that it would go into effect in 90 days from the date of signature. Since it was signed on August 7 of this year, it will go into effect on November 7, 1987. At that time all the provisions should go into effect simultaneously. In other words, the signatories to the agreement should be prepared to restore democratic rights as a cease-fire takes effect and amnesty should be given to all the opponents at the same time.
I failed to mention at the outset that the Five signatories to this agreement are different from the countries involved in the Contadora process. While the resolution refers to the Contadora process, it is to a certain extent out of date because

September 1, 1987
Peace in Central America
there were more countries involved, and in that case different countries. Here we have involved the five principal countries: Nicaragua, Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica, with the plan having been put forward by the President of Costa Rica, Oscar Arias.
Of course, Canada has given support to this peace agreement. As was mentioned by the representative of the Government, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has already offered assistance to the signatories to the agreement in implementing the process, in providing assistance for verification and for monitoring and so on. This is all to the good.
However, I do not think that the principal problem is now with the five signatories to the agreement, or with Canada's effort, but will be with the United States. The United States has been, and I think continues to be, the principal road-block to peace in that area. I should make it clear that I am talking about the Government of the United States and not the Congress or the people of the United States. Just after the signature of this agreement on August 7, these words appeared in The New York Times of August 16, "President Reagan said today that American support for the Nicaraguan rebels should continue until a cease-fire has occurred and a verifiable process of democratization is under way in that Central American country". So President Reagan says that there must be a certain type of democratization in Nicaragua, if there is going to be a cease-fire, a stoppage of the assistance to the Contras, but he does not mention Salvador. He does not mention Guatemala. He does not put any demands on them to live up to certain conditions of democracy or else the agreement should not be supported. However, he puts this on Nicaragua in particular.
The President of the United States has done that all along. All along he has said to Nicaragua, "Either you live up to the standards of democracy that we are dictating to you or we will continue to intervene in your affairs. We will continue to fund the Contras". The President of the United States has laid a standard of democracy on Nicaragua that he does not lay on other countries with which he deals.
He does not insist on those conditions of democracy for Chile, for example. He does not lay those conditions on South Africa. Nor does he lay them on China, a communist country with which he deals consistently and with which he has been quite friendly of late. However, with respect to little Nicaragua, which is about the size of New Brunswick and which has a population of fewer than three million people, he insists that it live up to very high standards of democracy. We would all like to have pure systems of democracy, and we all hope to move in that direction. The President of Nicaragua has stated that he, too, would like to move in that direction.
This is rather odd for the United States, a country which is celebrating I am not certain what anniversary of its Constitution in Philadelphia, which took until 1954-some 150 years after the birth of that nation-for blacks to have the vote.
Here is a country with only a two-Party system. It is almost impossible for a third Party to get elected in the United States. Yet that country is insisting that Nicaragua be a pluralist society, when in fact in the Nicaraguan Parliament there are five or six Parties represented because it has a system of proportional representation.
We can be a bit arrogant and a bit holier-than-thou when we start dictating to other countries that they should live up to standards of democracy that we ourselves have failed to live up to and that we do not insist upon for other countries. I refer here to the United States' dealings with South Africa, Chile, Nicaragua when Somoza was there, and the Philippines in previous times, and so on.
It seems to me that this peace agreement arrived at by the countries in the region with good faith will succeed if the United States, and in particular the President of the United States, will give it their support.
My plea in Parliament is not to the Government, because I think it is doing the correct thing in supporting the agreement, but my plea is to the United States Government to please give peace a chance in Central America, and in particular in Nicaragua, El Salvador, and Guatemala, and to help those countries to proceed with the agreement that they arrived at. Please stop the funding of the Contras until the Government of Nicaragua is given a fair chance to do what it states it will do in the agreement. Do not fund the Contras through the back door when it cannot be done through the front door, as was found out in recent months during the great television extravaganza in the United States Congress.
I congratulate the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) for introducing the resolution last June. At that time there was no peace agreement proposed by President Arias which is now agreed to. That was not in effect then, but the Hon. Member's proposals are still legitimate. Canada must do all it can to support peace in Central America. The proposals of the Hon. Member are worth-while. Please let us convince the American Government to support this worth-while peace agreement in that region.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING PEACE IN CENTRAL AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government believes that the fundamental causes of tension and political conflicts in Central America are the deeply rooted socioeconomic disparities that are rampant to various degrees in each and every country in this area.
In the Government's view, Canada can contribute the most to promoting peace and stability in those areas by first providing for development assistance aimed at helping individuals and communities break the vicious circle of poverty and promote economic growth, and, secondly, by supporting a peace settlement for that area.

September 1, 1987

Other speakers have already referred to the support Canada has been and is still providing for the efforts towards reaching such a settlement.
I would like to take a few moments to point out to this House the help Canada is providing to the people of Central America. Canadian development assistance in Central America was initiated in 1966 with a loan to El Salvador. After the 1970 foreign policy review, when it was recommended that Canada intensify its presence in the area, assistance activities were undertaken in all the countries of the area. Following the regional program review in 1975, El Salvador and Honduras became program countries for CIDA. In 1979, the planning of new bilateral projects in El Salvador was suspended because of increasing violence and instability in that country. In 1981, the planning of new, bilateral projects in Guatemala also was suspended by reason of internal turmoil in that country.
In 1982, after an in-depth review of the relations between Canada and Central America, the Government decided to extend substantially its development assistance program for countries in that region. For instance, the Government decided to provide up to $106 million in bilateral Government to Government assistance to the region during the five year period between 1982-83 and 1986-87, which is triple the amount of bilateral assistance provided to the region during the previous five-year period.
As for the countries which would benefit from this assistance, it was decided that Honduras, the poorest country in Central America, would rank first as in the past. Costa Rica and Nicaragua would also receive increased assistance, while Guatemala and El Salvador would continue not to receive any assistance until their domestic situation improved. However, all countries in the region could receive assistance through other channels. This would include the Mission Administered Funds Program, the Non-Governmental Organizations Program, the Institutional Cooperation Program, the Industrial Cooperation Program, the Humanitarian Assistance Program and the International Development Research Centre.
In December 1984, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Right Hon. Joe Clark, announced reinstatement of Government-to-Government assistance to El Salvador. This decision was made because of the needs of thousands of displaced people, of the economic under-development of El Salvador, of a noted improvement in the respect of human rights in that country and of its return to democratic institutions.
In the five-year period between 1982-83 and 1986-87, or since the Government decided to increase substantially its assistance to Central America, Canada has extended approximately $106 million in Government-to-Government assistance to the population of this region. In other words, the Canadian Government has kept its commitment of tripling bilateral assistance to the region.
Peace in Central America
However, the amount of assistance provided is only part of the picture. The quality and effectiveness of this assistance are at least as important.
We firmly believe that Canadians bilateral assistance to Central America effectively meets the development needs and problems of the various countries in the region. In Honduras, Canadian Government-to-Government assistance supports the development and protection of renewable resources, rural job creation and the improvement of health care and food supplies in rural regions. In Costa Rica, this assistance has been used to improve a very unhealthy balance of payments and to finance a major rural housing program. In Nicaragua, bilateral assistance provided by Canada has been directed mostly toward basic human needs, such as the production of food and energy. In El Salvador, this assistance is directed especially at displaced persons and the poorest members of the population.
Besides Government-to-Government assistance, Canada has provided over the past five years more than $45 million in aid to Central American countries through such other direct assistance channels as the Non-Governmental Organizations Program, the Institutional Cooperation Programme, the Business Cooperation Program, the Petro Canada International Assistance Corporation and the International Development Research Centre.
Also, for the past five years, Canada has provided more than $15 million to multilateral organizations such as the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and the International Committee of the Red Cross for the programs they have developed to help refugees and displaced persons in Central America.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly believe that Canada, through its public development assistance programs, meets generously and effectively the social and economic needs of the peoples in Central America. This is one of the regions of the world where Canada provides the highest per capita public development assistance. The Canadian Government and people will continue to meet generously the social and economic needs of the peoples in Central America.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING PEACE IN CENTRAL AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to have this opportunity to debate the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap).
The motion addresses a very difficult and complex situation which exists in Central America. This is an important issue, because Central America is the scene of some of the most tragic warfare in the world today, and it also has become the scene of serious East-West conflict. It is important to Canada because it is taking place in the western hemisphere, in that part of the Third World closest to Canada, and in a region with which Canada has growing social, economic, and political interests.
The emergence of a new peace plan which has been described, and the initiative of the countries of Central

September 1, 1987
Peace in Central America
America themselves are the most encouraging development in the region for several years. As has already been pointed out, the Canadian Government has not stood idly by during those years. While recognizing that Canada has no direct role to play at this stage of the negotiations, we have gone to some lengths to give the maximum possible support and encouragement to the parties. The process of converting the commitments which have been made into a peace settlement will be a difficult one. Our support is more than rhetorical. The Government stands ready to provide technical advice, where it has the appropriate expertise to offer in the control and verification process which will follow a cease-fire in the region.
1 wish to remind the House, however, that this is not a new approach by the Government. On the contrary, it is entirely consistent with the policies which the Government has pursued with respect to Central America since it was elected. Indeed, our recent effort in support of the new peace plan is a logical extension of the role Canada has sought to play for some time.
Canadian policy toward Central America is a distinct one, shaped by Canadian criteria. It has been developed in recognition of the geo-political realities of Central America and of the social and economic factors which are at the root of the current problems.
The Canadian Government opposes third party intervention anywhere in Central America and regrets deeply the intrusion into that region of East-West tensions and the related militarization of the area. Canada does not approve of the supply of armaments by any country to opposing factions in the region. Canada has constantly emphasized its firm belief that the countries of Central America must be free to seek their own solutions to their own problems without interference from any other country or any outside source.
We strongly share the view that the growth and development of democracy is an important issue in Central America. Canada welcomes the progress which has been made in several countries in the region while recognizing that there is still room for improvement.
We in Canada do not wish to see Nicaragua locked into the Soviet bloc or involved in destabilizing its neighbours. We encourage Nicaragua to move toward the original goals of the revolution which were recently restated in its new Constitution: a commitment to political pluralism, a mixed economy and non-intervention in the internal affairs of other countries.
We believe that improvements must be made in the Nicaraguan civil and human rights record. The continued suspension of many basic civil rights under the state of emergency is profoundly disturbing to the people of Canada and Canada's Government. We encourage political pluralism in Nicaragua and we support the ability of legitimate domestic political opposition Parties to continue to function.
We have deplored the recent decision to close down La Prensa newspaper and the harassment of opposition groups and of churches. The recent arrest and sentencing of the head of the Nicaraguan Human Rights Commission and the head of the Nicaraguan Bar Association within days of the signing of the peace accord was a disturbing and potentially counterproductive development. It was not consistent with the spirit of the agreement and only served to emphasize the need for reforms within Nicaragua.
We hope that the implementation of the peace plan will result in the lifting of the state of emergency, the removal of current restrictions on the press and opposition groups, and an end to incidents such as that to which I have referred.
In conclusion, let me reiterate the Government's satisfaction that negotiations for a peaceful settlement in Central America are under way again. We are under no illusions about the obstacles which lie in the way of a just peace, but Canada stands ready to do what it can to support the process.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF PROMOTING PEACE IN CENTRAL AMERICA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in closing the debate today, I would like to take the opportunity to thank the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) for bringing forward his resolution. I think we all know of his many years of interest in and concern for this issue and of his experience and involvement in Central America. I know it is a concern shared by many Canadians and indeed by the Government.
I appreciate the support of the Hon. Member for Spadina in the efforts of the Government in Central America over the past few years. Indeed, as other colleagues have said, we welcome the new peace agreement, but I would just like to say that that agreement was not easily won. It did not happen overnight and it was preceded by many years of hard work and by many disappointments. It was an important breakthrough, but there are many difficulties in the way of implementation and a great deal of hard work and good faith, both within and outside the region, will be essential to make it happen.
I would like to summarize briefly each of the four specific points made by the Hon. Member in his resolution. First, as he indicated and as other Hon. Members have already said, we have already sent two senior officials to the region to do precisely what the Hon. Member has suggested that a personal envoy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) should do. Their trip has indeed reinforced Canada's diplomatic efforts in the region and their message has been warmly received by all Central American Governments, including the Nicaraguan Government.
Second, while the Government would certainly like to have an embassy in Nicaragua, as it would in many other places, it is unable to do so for financial reasons. We cannot have embassies in every part of the world, and we have existing arrangements which are working very well for us and will proceed for the time being.
The establishment of a peace fund was proposed by my
colleague. As Hon. Members are aware, Canada has already
September 1, 1987

contributed significantly to bilateral development assistance and to multilateral efforts. In per capita terms, the amount of Canadian aid to Central America is considerable. Canadian aid to the region is given for developmental and compassionate reasons. It also serves to complement the Contadora peace objectives.
Finally, the proposal for the civilian monitoring commission has obviously been overtaken by the new peace agreement. What form the monitoring of the cease-fire will take is obviously up to the Central American Governments, but the Canadian Government has already taken constructive action in support of the peace agreement and offered its technical assistance and advice.
I think it is appropriate, in concluding, to summarize what has been said about Canada's policies and role in Central America as this is the main thrust of the resolution before the House. I believe that the suggestion that Canada is not doing enough is wrong. That suggestion is perhaps implicit in the resolution and the comments we have heard.
Canadians have been very active in the region for many years. We have observed closely the developments in the region. We have spoken out on issues as an informed and sympathetic observer to do wherever it has been appropriate for us to do so. Canada's voice has been loud and clear on many issues, including the external involvement in the region and the inappropriateness of seeking military solutions. There has been encouragement for negotiations and for human rights.
Canada has built up a large aid program carefully designed to meet the most pressing needs of the poorest people of the region. We have encouraged trade with the region because we believe that economic development is one of the most effective means of combatting the fundamental social and economic problems. We have provided active support for negotiations in the region by giving technical advice when required to do so.
This distinctly Canadian approach to Central America has been shown clearly in our prompt, positive reaction to the recently agreed to peace program. Canada expressed its strong support for the plan immediately after it was announced and followed up with visits by officials to capitals in the region. We have also renewed our offer to provide technical advice on verification and control.
As Hon. Members may recall, in a period of less than two weeks, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) issued three statements. The first was a message of support on the very eve of the Central American summit. Then he issued a statement reporting on the congratulatory messages he had sent to the Central American Governments. He also reported on statements relating to his decision to send officials to the region. This is indicative not only of the Minister's personal interest but also of his determination that Canada should react positively and constructively to these events.
Adjournment Debate
As the hour draws near, I would hope that all Hon. Members on all sides of the House would join me in congratulating the Government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for the strong, supportive stand taken toward countries in the troubled region of Central America and in urging the Government to continue to do all in its power to assist those countries in achieving a peaceful resolution to their disputes.

ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-LENGTH OF PRISON SENTENCES-GRANTING OF PAROLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 24, 1987, I rose in this House to ask a question of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) regarding problems with the justice system in Canada. 1 was concerned about the Government's efforts in this area now that the question of capital punishment has been settled.
The amount of public outcry generated by the issue of capital punishment was a clear indication that Canadians are not satisfied with safety in our society and our justice system. Both supporters and opponents of the reinstatement of capital punishment agreed that there is a real need for reform. I am concerned, as are my constituents of Don Valley East, that prison terms are too lenient and parole is being granted too early in too many instances.
I was pleased with the Minister's response to my question on these two issues that the Government is, indeed, concerned with this problem and that steps are being taken to improve the sentencing and parole systems. I would like, however, to emphasize how strong Canadians feel about violent criminals and the inadequacies of our justice system in protecting innocent citizens.
According to a poll released by Maclean's magazine on June 29, 1987, 87 per cent of those questioned believe convicted murderers are allowed back into society too soon. The poll also indicates that the large majority of Canadians are deeply troubled by a rising incidence of murder and other violent crimes. The Canadian public has lost a great deal of faith in our criminal justice system.

September 1, 1987
Adjournment Debate
The Canadian Sentencing Commission has reported a number of serious problems with sentencing in Canada. One of the basic problems it listed was a lack of public confidence in sentencing. The public's negative perceptions have led to some people taking the law into their own hands. Out of frustration and a belief that the justice system has failed them, many Canadian citizens are arming themselves and seeking their own methods of punishing criminals. A noted example of this is the recent case in Calgary of Mr. Steven Kesler, who shot a man who was attempting to rob him. If the public's confidence in our justice system is not improved quickly, I am afraid we will see more and more instances of vigilante type actions from the public.
The Canadian Sentencing Commission links some of the problems with the sentencing system to the "almost complete absence of policy from Parliament on the principles that should govern the determination of sentences". It also credits "parole and early release programs that fail to accomplish their goals" as well as "unrealistic maximum and minimum penalties that create injustices". I know that no justice system is infallible, Mr. Speaker, but it seems clear to me that our own system is in desperate need of improvements.
I am sure we are all familiar with the case of Ms. Celia Ruygrok whose tragic murder was an example of the justice system failing completely. Ms. Ruygrok was sexually assaulted and murdered by a man on parole after being convicted of a similar murder. He had violated his parole and threatened his former girlfriend just weeks before Celia's murder. However, due to confusion and a lack of communication, Celia's murderer was allowed his freedom and Celia Ruygrok was denied her right to live.
Just today, by coincidence, I received a letter from the President of Victims of Violence expressing concern that criminals with a history of violence are released back into the community after serving only a fraction of their sentences. The victims of these crimes feel that the justice system is cheating them. The residents of Don Valley East have made it clear to me that they want to see some government action. I would like to quote some of my constituents thoughts on this issue.
Earl and Winnifred Miller of Denrock Drive wrote: "We were in favour of the death penalty. If nothing else, the argument for retention has made Parliament aware that the majority of Canadians are fed up with our lax judicial system and want something done to improve it. Even abolitionists have had to admit that something is wrong and needs correcting."
Andrew and Audrey Mathews of Graydon Hall Drive wrote: "Parliament should be grappling with ways of answering the anger, anguish, suffering and material loss of those who are crime's victims".
Mr. Blair Kingsland of Cassandra Boulevard wrote: "I
believe that my rights to live and breathe as a law-abiding
Canadian citizen should be respected and protected before the rights of criminals."
Fred and Sue Olds of Wellesbourne Crescent wrote in reference to first degree murderers: "In our opinion, the problem would be better served with life sentences that mean life sentences with no parole."
Ms. Wendy Spencer of Yellow Birchway wrote: "I am convinced that our parole system is irrational and ridiculous and thus requires an immediate overhaul. It needs to be tightened up. It is ludicrous to allow dangerously violent people to roam the streets on passes."
And finally, Ms. Jean Dodds of Kestell Lane wrote: "There is, as you know, a glaring lack of rationale in both sentencing and parole and the intelligent voter is not only angry but alarmed at the disparities and injustices."
My constituents, indeed most Canadians, are demanding action. When Members of this House voted against reinstatement of capital punishment, we accepted the responsibility of developing alternative solutions to protect the Canadian public from violent criminals, and more specifically, repeat offenders.
I would like to emphasize the gravity of this issue and ask that the Government respond to the recommendations of the Canadian Sentencing Commission and the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General as soon as they are made available. The Canadian public expects us to make every effort to protect their rights and freedoms. I hope it will not take another tragic event like Celia Ruygrok's murder to realize that, up until now, our efforts have been too little, too late.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his question the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Attewell) mentioned that many Canadians feel the sentences handed down are too lenient.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the Hon. Member is aware of the increasing number of sociological studies that have shown that Canadians who are sufficiently informed feel that the sentences handed down by the courts are severe enough and would even be inclined to be more lenient than the courts.
On March 25 this year, our esteemed Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Hnatyshyn) tabled in Parliament the report of the Canadian Sentencing Commission. This report is said to be the first comprehensive study of sentencing ever carried out in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I am informed that legal experts at the Department of Justice are proceeding with another series of consultations and extensive discussions on the recommendations of this report. When the process is complete, the Minister of Justice will be in a position to consider any changes that may be necessary to improve the effectiveness of the Canadian sentencing system.
September 1, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I believe you yourself are an expert in this field. In addition to examining the recommendations of the Sentencing Commission, this fall the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General will also consider the difficult question of parole.
And once again the recommendations contained in Judge Archambault's report will be considered, as will the merit of a parole system and the wisdom of the existing legislation under which it operates, including for example the regulations which set the jail term to be served by an inmate before he may become eligible for the various forms of parole.
The committee Members will scrutinize the wisdom of this legislation and the merit of the parole system. Still, Mr. Speaker, we must keep in mind the fact that sentencing and parole questions are closely related and that if any major change were to be made to the parole system it would have to be reflected in rules governing sentencing.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the whole matter is still under consideration and a report will be made public in due time.

subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-MAXIMUM SENTENCE FOR MURDER-REQUEST THAT STATUTE BE AMENDED
YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-MAXIMUM SENTENCE FOR MURDER-REQUEST THAT STATUTE BE AMENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that you may not be aware of a murder case that occurred in Port Credit, a small community near Metropolitan Toronto in the Mississauga area in May, 1985. That was a case of the murder of a mother, Paulina Zerger, and her 11-year old daughter Tanya. As a result of that case two charges of first degree murder were laid against a youth who was only 15 years old at the time. The youth was charged with murder under the Young Offenders Act.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, there is a provision under the Young Offenders Act that the Crown Attorney may move to have a murder case moved up to adult court for trial. You may recall that a year or two ago that was a very controversial thing, at least in the Province of Ontario where, in a number of instances, a motion was not made to move the case up to adult court, the cases were tried in Young Offenders Court and, as a result, there was a great deal of criticism about the fact that the penalty provided for in the Young Offenders Act was too lenient in the case of a serious offence.
As a result of that, the Attorney General for the Province of Ontario gave instructions at that time to all of his Crown Attorneys, in every case of murder or a violent crime in which someone was charged under the Young Offenders Act, to make a motion to move those charges up to adult court. That has been the policy and procedure followed in recent months in the Province of Ontario.
In the Zerger murder case that motion was made by the Crown Attorney. The trial court judge granted the motion and allowed it to be moved up to adult court, but that decision was
Adjournment Debate
appealed to the Ontario Court of Appeal because the penalty for murder in an adult court which the young person faced was 25 years imprisonment subject, of course, to the recent Chartrand decision which might make him eligible for parole after only 15 years. In the Young Offenders Act the maximum sentence for a murder conviction is only three years.
The decision was appealed and the Court of Appeal for the Province of Ontario reversed the trial court's decision. In doing so the late Associate Chief Justice of the Ontario Court of Appeal, Bert MacKinnon, said that when Parliament passed the Young Offenders Act in 1984, it must have intended that young people convicted of serious crimes would serve shorter sentences than adults.
That begs the question as to whether a young person between the ages of 12 and 18, in this particular case 15 years of age, when charged with first degree murder of two people, one of them being an 11-year old girl, should be facing a penalty of a maximum term of imprisonment of only three years or a maximum term of imprisonment of 25 years as they would be if they had reached adulthood and not been subject to the Young Offenders Act in the first place.
The Deputy Director of the Crown Law Office for the Ontario Attorney General has indicated that he believes that a three-year sentence is not long enough to protect the public in the case of a young offender convicted of murder.
I do not know about your constituents, Mr. Speaker, but my constituents certainly agree with the Deputy Director of the Crown Law Office. That is certainly the indication they have given me, not only in this case but in many other cases of a similar nature.
It is interesting to note as well that one of the major Toronto newspapers, The Toronto Star, indicated editorially that the Young Offenders Act should be amended to provide for a maximum sentence for a young offender of five, six, or seven years in the case of murder in order to avoid the appearance of too lenient sentences.
Even more interesting, the lawyer for this particular young offender in the Zerger case said after the trial and the Court of Appeal had reversed the lower court and sent it back to the young offenders court, that he did not feel that a three-year term was long enough. He felt that a term of eight to nine years would be more appropriate in the case of a young offender convicted of first degree murder.
In 1986, the Young Offenders Act was amended by the present Government. At that time there were a number of amendments introduced and it was indicated that if further amendments were necessary the Government was certainly prepared to consider those. In my view, it is time that the Government began to consider these further changes. For one thing, it certainly should be considering changes in the maximum penalty for a young offender convicted of first

September 1, 1987
Adjournment Debate
degree murder. If the courts will not let these proceed in adult court, surely we must make changes in the Young Offenders Act.
A second area that must be addressed is one that has been commented on by the Ontario high school principals and teachers association. It is the case of not being able to identify a young offender, thereby leaving the schools caught in the middle. According to the law, a young offender must attend school but cannot be identified to teachers and principals. Of course, they are concerned for the safety of the students and staff.
Finally, there is the area of offenders under the age of 12, which has been a controversial issue for some time. In the Province of Ontario, the public does not understand why a person under the age of 12 is not subject to the Young Offenders Act, particularly when there were 1,855 children under 12 involved in serious crimes in Metropolitan Toronto alone in 1985.
All of these areas need changes. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will indicate tonight on behalf of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), who is now responsible for the Young Offenders Act, that there will be some changes soon in this legislation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: YOUNG OFFENDERS ACT-MAXIMUM SENTENCE FOR MURDER-REQUEST THAT STATUTE BE AMENDED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our very compassionate Minister of Justice (M. Hnatyshyn), 1 am happy to reply to the excellent question of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) about what is certainly a burning issue.
The Young Offenders Act has established a modern framework for the Canadian juvenile justice system. Several aspects of this legislation are innovative and have therefore given rise to much debate, both before and after its coming into force in 1982.
However, it is generally admitted that this Act constitutes a proper and balanced response to juvenile crime. For instance, the Young Offenders Act recognizes that the juvenile justice system created by the legislation is not always appropriate and that, in certain cases, serious criminal cases should be judged by the adult courts.
The Act provides a mechanism to transfer certain charges to the adult court, where the young offender is judged in accordance with the Criminal Code and is liable to the same penalties as an adult.
A transfer hearing is held when the Crown, or even the accused, in some cases, so requests, and the judge must consider several factors, such as the seriousness of the offence, the background of the accused and the existence of a previous criminal record.
During the consultations which led to the tabling of Bill
C-106, which was debated and passed by this House in 1986,
the then Solicitor General proposed some amendments to the transfer provisions of the legislation. More precisely, he proposed that the age at which trial could be moved up to adult court be lowered from 14 to 12 years old-which is very sad but, alas, realistic-and that for the most serious crimes there be, automatically, a hearing on the move up. These proposals where withdrawn following objections from authorities in the area of justice for the young, most notably provincial Solicitors General and Ministers of Justice.
Mr. Speaker, provincial authorities concluded that the move up clauses in the old Act and in the new one were more appropriate. The efficiency of the Act and of each of its clauses will continue to be carefully monitored and to be the subject of consultations by our Government in general and our Minister of Justice in particular, in order to keep our legislation in tune with the most recent needs and to take care of these unfortunate young people in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight 1 would like to have answers. I was not satisfied with the one that was given to me by the then Minister of Finance on the amendments to his last budget and also on tax reform. 1 think it is important for each and everyone of us, and the Parliamentary Secretary, to remember that, at that time, the Government announced it was amending the income tax exemptions and converting them into tax credits.
We welcome that initiative because such was the recommendation made by the Liberal Party and by all groups who worked with the committee on consultation on social program reform, and it will be remembered unfortunately that at that point the Prime Minister misled both our senior citizens and families when he said that he would reinstate full indexation of old age security pensions and that the changes to the family income support program would not be used to reduce the deficit but rather to increase benefits to those who are most in need. We will remember unfortunately the attempt to partially deindex old age security pensions and, thanks to the Official Opposition and senior citizens, the Government's change of heart.
Next, through deindexing of family allowances, the Government will have cut as much as one billion dollars by 1991, preferring to use this money to lower the deficit and bail out the depositors with over $60,000 invested in a couple of Western Canada banking establishments.
We had agreed to replace the tax exemption with a tax credit, but it is unfortunately a non-refundable tax credit. Which means that a person who has not enough income will not be entitled to this tax credit, and there are as many as 1.4 million senior citizens in Canada who, in his last budget, will not be able to benefit from this tax credit. Hon. Members will
September 1, 1987

remember that yesterday, the Forum of Senior Citizens, on the basis of a study it carried out on the tax policies which this Government has implemented in its budgets since September 4, 1984, clearly established that senior citizens and low and middle income families have been greatly affected. Also, the study of the Carleton University report clearly indicates that these people have been greatly affected compared with the more affluent.
I should like to know if the Parliamentary Secretary could further explain why this is not a refundable tax credit which replaced the old age exemption. Moreover, the Forum of Senior Citizens indicated that the $1,000 income deduction under a RRSP or a retirement-oriented investment would greatly affect senior citizens which now benefit from it, and that it was not replaced by a refundable tax credit. I dare hope, therefore, that the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to provide the right answer, not so much to the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie, but especially to the senior citizens who are listening to us and who would like to know whether the Government will grant them a refundable tax credit, and also whether it will join the Liberal Party in its campaign to oppose a tax on bread, milk and butter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: TAX REFORM-FUTURE OF MINISTER OF FINANCE-OLD AGE EXEMPTION-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Right away, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that I am not going to join in such shadow boxing. For the leader of our party, who is also the leader of the Government, clearly indicated in the House this afternoon that this issue was thoroughly dealt with, and that we are not going to restrict the normal consultation of the Canadian people by limiting the debate and providing ready-made answers. When this Conservative Government seeks the advice of the people, Mr. Speaker, it offers them all necessary options and we believe that the Canadian people is adult enough to tell right from wrong.
However, Mr. Speaker, let me just give him and all senior citizens a few examples-in answer to the specific request made by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte Marie (Mr. Malepart)-of how to deal with fiscal reform. It is estimated for example that personal exemptions in 1988 will reach some $2,700. For taxpayers with incomes below $27,500, for example, who are quite numerous . . . That is to say, for that category of taxpayers who are uppermost in the mind of the Hon. Member, the rate of tax would be 17 percent. The value
Adjournment Debate
of the tax exemption for senior citizens would therefore come to some $454. In its place, the Government has opted for a tax credit of $550, which represents about $100 more. This means the tax break has improved by some 20 percent.
Mr. Speaker, another example can be given here. As indicated in the tables on pages 51 and 52 of the document on income tax reform, which deal with typical taxpayers, single persons and couples aged over 65 benefit substantially from tax reform. The tables show that income tax changes brought about by fiscal reform will mean savings of some $430 for single persons and of some $825 for couples, and this will represents savings of as much as 66 percent compared to the taxes which they paid previously.
Let me give you another example, Mr. Speaker. The minimum taxable income level for senior citizens will rise from $10,800 to $11,500 for single persons, and from $16,000 to $19,000 for married couples. About 250,000 Canadians 65 years old or more will no longer pay any federal income tax.
For instance, the conversion of the $1,000 pension income deduction to a credit of 17 per cent will have the same value for older peole whose income is less than $27,500, that is more than 80, per cent of senior citizens who file income tax returns.
I would like to give you a last example, Mr. Speaker. Low income senior citizens will benefit in 1988 from the higher sales tax refund which will be upped from $50 et $70 per adult.
Mr. Speaker, we have loads of other examples. The White Paper on Tax Reform proposes all kinds of increased tax exemptions, tax savings aimed particularly at senior citizens. They should be presented as they are, and some incidental parts should not be blown out of proportion and distorted from a purely political perspective. Scare tactics should stop. Our people, those of my beautiful riding of LaSalle are certainly better informed than that. Let me tell you that they are not taken in by false and vague theoretical promises. They put greater confidence in dollar savings such as those the future tax reform will bring them.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a very short point of order on which I would like to seek some guidance from the Chair. It is with regard to the situation which arose late in the day yesterday. Members of
the House had been informed earlier in the day that there would be a vote called at six o'clock as per the Standing Orders. The Standing Orders provide for a 15-minute bell in that case.
I would like to make the point that Members of Parliament work not only in the House of Commons giving presentations and voting at the appropriate time, but also carry on their responsibilities and duties in standing, special and joint committees as well as carrying out their regular responsibilities as Members of Parliament. In order to do that effectively it is important that Members have the opportunity to schedule their day's events.
This is not an earth-shattering situation and I do not want to suggest that it is. However, we have Standing Orders so that we can understand what we are doing here. The reform committee which studied this matter for a considerable length of time made its recommendations in order to facilitate the business of the House of Commons so that Members of the House would have a clear understanding of what was transpiring at any time.
I draw this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, because you were conducting business elsewhere at the pertinent time last night. I thought it would be appropriate for you to make a comment at the appropriate time. Members were assembled at the appropriate time for the vote and five minutes passed and then 10 minutes and then 15 minutes. It is understandable that Members of Parliament became concerned. After the vote a number of people asked me, as House Leader of the New Democrats, why we waited for so long.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, this is not the most important event in Canada today, but if we are going to facilitate the business of the House and take it seriously, it is important that rules, regulations, conventions and traditions be followed unless there is good reason to depart from them after discussion and concurrence of the Parties involved. I draw that to your attention, Mr. Speaker, to reflect the view of my Party that there was concern that the business and planning of a number of Members in my caucus, and I suspect in all caucuses, was disrupted yesterday. At the appropriate time I would appreciate a comment from the Chair on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order. Actually, I tried to raise this point of order yesterday afternoon, after the bells had rung for more than fifteen minutes. However, I was unable to do so because we were in a vacuum. The bells were ringing and no one could speak in the House.
The point I want to make is that in Standing Order 13(2) which is very clear, we read the following:
(2) When, under the provisions of any Standing Order or other Order of this House, the Speaker has interrupted any proceeding for the purpose of putting forthwith the question on any business then before the House, the bells to call in the Members shall be sounded for not more than fifteen minutes.
The first question that comes to mind is why the bells had not stopped, since they were supposed to stop. The Standing Orders are clear. 1 may remind Hon. Members that before the Standing Orders were amended, the bells could go on ringing for an indefinite period. There were times when opposition parties took advantage of this fact and prolonged the ringing of the bells to make a certain point, and this has occasionally created a chaotic political situation in this country.
When our Party negotiated with the Government to amend the Standing Orders of the House, we agreed to a time limit on the ringing of the bells, fully realizing that this would put certain constraints on an opposition party that would no longer have the means of using the bells to get its point across. Since we as the Opposition Party agreed to discipline ourselves and to change the Standing Orders, thus losing a mechanism, in fact a weapon, it could otherwise have used in the House, I think it is only fair that the Government should observe the Standing Orders, since they apply to both the Government and the Opposition.
I realize that according to our parliamentary tradition, the bell stops ringing when the Whips enter side by side and walk onto the floor of the House.
However, the Standing Order I read earlier is quite clear: The bells shall ring for not more than fifteen minutes.
1 think that, eventually, the Chair should make a statement in the House-at least that is what I would suggest-to clarify the interpretation of this Standing Order so that all Members know what the situation is. That is what I would urge you to do, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I simply want to add a short comment in response to the Hon. Minister's intervention. It concerns the fact that this is one of the Standing Orders that has not been abused, as he has indicated. From time to time there is accommodation made. I think it is important that we recognize that for this particular vote to which we are referring in the deliberations this morning, Members and Party Whips had three days notice. It was not as though the motion and the vote came as a surprise. When that does happen, often we end up voting very quickly and accommodations are made back and forth, as I hope they will be from now on.
Considering the advance notice that all Parties had, and the advance recognition that there would be a vote at six o'clock and the bells would ring until 6.15, I simply thought it was appropriate that we follow the rules of the House of Commons under those conditions.

subtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH S. O. 13(2)-EXTENSION OF BELLS

The Hon Parliamentary Secretary.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I certainly do not want to violate the rules of the House. speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH S. O. 13(2)-EXTENSION OF BELLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order. 1 cannot stand the allusions being made by the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister. If they want to know the truth, let them ask the Government Whip why he was not in the House. He knows why, and I know why, and I will say so. I know the reason.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH S. O. 13(2)-EXTENSION OF BELLS
speechtext: Order. I fully understand what the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) is saying. I also know why he is saying it. But I think that we probably do not need a lot of comments about the absence of Members, whether they belong to the Government or the Official Opposition or to the New Democratic Party.

subtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH S. O. 13(2)-EXTENSION OF BELLS
speechtext:
The Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons of the House went to a great deal of trouble to eliminate that possibility. One of the ways in which we were to eliminate that possibility was by having a 15 minute bell when the bell would ring for 15 minutes and then there would be a vote, and if there was a 30 minute bell, the bells would ring for 30 minutes and then there would be a vote.
This point of order is not over nothing; it is about something which could be very dangerous. I say that to Members because they know it. I could see it on their faces last night. They knew what was happening. This should not happen again. It is as simple as that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMPLIANCE WITH S. O. 13(2)-EXTENSION OF BELLS
speechtext:
The matter that has been raised this morning was brought to my attention earlier today and I very deeply regret that it happened. I will consider carefully what Hon. Members from all three Parties have said. I do want to reiterate that there is a tradition in this place that sometimes the Chair is guided by the disposition of the Whips. That is a tradition which we may well not want to abolish completely.
However, the extension of the bells last night was lengthy. I think the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) probably, if he had been less inclined to be the gentleman he is, might have indicated at least part of the reason for that extension. I think Hon. Members perhaps know that part of the reason for that extension was a courtesy extended in the best traditions of this place to those from one Party to another.
The point that has been raised I take seriously and I will come back with some comments which I hope will be of some guidance to the House, without at the same time being so severe that Whips among themselves will be constrained from exercising upon occasion some appropriate common sense.
What happened last night was regrettable, and I am very sorry it happened. 1 will do everything I can to ensure that it does not happen again. I will come back with some measured comments which I hope will be accepted by all Members of the House. I thank all Members for intervening this morning. Their comments were helpful to the Chair.
